title: Tibial spine avulsion fracture: anterior cruciate ligament
vignette: A 17-year-old boy comes to the office with right knee pain after being tackled in rugby the previous day. He has difficulty bearing weight, and it feels as if his knee is unstable. On examination, a large effusion is present, and the patient has limited range of motion due to pain. X-ray of the right knee demonstrates an avulsion fracture of the tibial spine (the bony eminence on the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia), with the avulsed fragment detached together with the ligament that inserts there. Injury to which of the following structures is most likely present in this patient?

clues.text: tackled in rugby the previous day
clues.note: A twisting/valgus force during a tackle in a skeletally immature athlete is the classic mechanism. In adolescents the incompletely ossified tibial eminence is weaker than the ligament, so the bone avulses instead of the ligament tearing mid-substance.

clues.text: it feels as if his knee is unstable
clues.note: Instability points to a ligamentous (cruciate) injury. The ACL resists anterior tibial translation and internal rotation; losing it produces the sensation of the knee giving way.
A rapid, large effusion after a pivot injury is a hemarthrosis - bleeding into the joint - which is characteristic of an ACL tear (or its bony-avulsion equivalent).

clues.text: avulsion fracture of the tibial spine
clues.note: The tibial spine (anterior intercondylar eminence) is the tibial INSERTION of the anterior cruciate ligament. An avulsion fracture here means the ACL pulled off its bony attachment - i.e., ACL disruption. This is the confirmatory finding.

whatMatters: The tibial spine (anterior intercondylar eminence) is the tibial insertion of the ACL. In a skeletally immature patient, a twisting/valgus tackle avulses that bony attachment rather than tearing the ligament mid-substance. Hemarthrosis (large effusion) + instability confirm ACL involvement. Answer A.
strategy: Convert the bony landmark into its soft-tissue attachment: tibial spine avulsion = ACL. Then match each distractor ligament to ITS attachment - PCL to the posterior intercondylar area (seen on lateral x-ray), MCL to the medial epicondyle/proximal tibia, LCL to the lateral epicondyle/fibular head, patellar tendon to the inferior patella/tibial tuberosity, and MPFL to the medial patella.

eliminations.label: Posterior cruciate ligament - posterior attachment
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the PCL attaches to the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia and resists posterior tibial translation. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: its avulsion appears on the POSTERIOR tibia (best seen on lateral x-ray), not at the anterior tibial spine, and PCL injuries are rarer (dashboard injury). ✅ Correct if: a posterior tibial avulsion or a dashboard/posterior-drawer mechanism.

eliminations.label: Medial collateral ligament - extraarticular, medial
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the MCL runs from the medial femoral epicondyle to the proximal medial tibia and resists valgus stress. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is extraarticular and attaches at the medial femur/tibia, not the central tibial spine; injury gives medial joint-line tenderness, not a spine avulsion. ✅ Correct if: valgus stress with medial joint-line tenderness.

eliminations.label: Lateral collateral ligament - extraarticular, lateral
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the LCL runs from the lateral femoral epicondyle to the fibular head and resists varus stress. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is extraarticular at the lateral femur/fibular head, away from the anterior midline tibial spine. ✅ Correct if: varus injury with an avulsion at the fibular head.

eliminations.label: Patellar tendon - inferior patella
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the patellar tendon runs from the inferior pole of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: its avulsion causes patella alta (a high-riding patella from unopposed quadriceps pull), not a tibial spine fracture. ✅ Correct if: the patella is displaced superiorly after injury.

eliminations.label: Patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) - patellar stabilizer
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the medial patellofemoral ligament connects the patella to the medial femoral epicondyle and stabilizes the patella. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is injured in LATERAL patellar dislocation (avulsion at the medial patella), unrelated to the tibial spine. ✅ Correct if: lateral patellar dislocation with a medial patellar avulsion.

reasoning: Tibial spine (anterior intercondylar eminence) = tibial insertion of the ACL
Skeletally immature bone fails before the ligament, so a twisting tackle avulses the spine rather than tearing the ACL mid-substance
Hemarthrosis (large effusion) + instability match ACL disruption
-> injury to the anterior cruciate ligament; answer A
mechanism: The anterior cruciate ligament originates on the posteromedial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and inserts on the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia - the tibial spine (eminence) - where it resists anterior translation of the tibia and internal tibial rotation. A sudden twisting or valgus force (as in a rugby tackle) loads the ACL in tension; in adolescents whose tibial eminence is not fully ossified, the bone fails before the ligament, producing an avulsion fracture of the tibial spine that carries the ACL attachment. The clinical picture - hemarthrosis (large effusion), pain-limited motion, and a feeling of instability - matches a mid-substance ACL tear. The other ligaments attach elsewhere (PCL posteriorly; MCL/LCL extraarticularly; patellar tendon at the inferior patella; MPFL at the medial patella), so they are not implicated by a tibial spine avulsion.

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid MSK/Anatomy > knee ligaments: ACL (anterior intercondylar tibia <- posteromedial lateral femoral condyle) resists anterior tibial translation; PCL, MCL, LCL, patellar tendon, MPFL attachments; pediatric tibial eminence avulsion = ACL equivalent.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: The stem gives a bony finding (tibial spine avulsion) and asks which soft-tissue structure is injured. Translate landmark -> attachment: tibial spine = ACL insertion.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on tibial spine/intercondylar eminence, avulsion fracture, hemarthrosis, cruciate vs collateral, or patella alta? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: The collaterals (MCL/LCL) and PCL are tempting 'knee ligament' picks, but only the ACL inserts at the anterior tibial spine. PCL is posterior; collaterals are extraarticular.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.message: On the x-ray, compare the normal knee to the avulsed bony fragment at the tibial spine (anterior intercondylar region) pulled up with the ACL. Anchor on 'fragment at the tibial eminence = ACL avulsion.'

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: tibial spine avulsion = ACL disruption; in kids the immature eminence avulses instead of the ligament tearing; hemarthrosis + instability.

memoryHook: The tibial SPINE is where the ACL sits down - avulse the spine, you avulse the ACL.
